utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue to -- with the examination of Witness DP35, the Chamber would like to give an opportunity to the Prosecution to raise the issues it intended yesterday to raise. Mr. Ierace, could you give us an impression on how much time you need to address the Chamber, because we have to consider whether we'll hear it all orally or that we would ask you to make a written submission. If you could please organise your intervention in such a way that you first indicate what issues you'd like to deal with, and we'll then see whether full opportunity will be given now or whether we'll ask you to submit any written filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two issues I would seek to raise immediately. They would take only a few minutes. We have not as a team completed our assessment of the impact of the course taken by the Defence, and therefore any remaining matters, I would be grateful if I could leave until perhaps Friday to address the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you need more time, you'll find the -- a moment in due course when to address the Chamber on this issue once the Prosecution has made up its mind as to its position. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I then at this stage raise those two matters which I anticipate should take only a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps that should be done in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then -- would private session be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be sufficient, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we could then continue the examination of the present witness, DP35. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Do the curtains have to be pulled down? Is that for the video -- is there anyone in the -- if it's just for the passage, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, before escorting the witness into the courtroom, would you please check that the public gallery is still empty. Also, if you escort the witness into the courtroom. So would you please then escort the witness into the courtroom. May I invite both parties to check whether there is an empty public gallery. Yes. This asks for a close cooperation between the two parties, one of them having an overview of half of the public gallery, the other party having an overview of the other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In fact, there is very little shared area, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. I ask the witness be shown document -- it is P3771. We have copies for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please place the document on the device to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If the ELMO may be panned back slightly so we can see the writing at the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have in front of you a bundle of photocopies of photographs. We see now on the screen the first of those images. Was this weapon one of those under your control; in other words, this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What did you refer to this weapon as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An anti-aircraft gun, 30 millimetres. M53 through 59, or rather, M59 through 63. It had certain modifications on the aiming device, and it was popularly called a Praga, because it was on a Praga vehicle. The vehicle that the weapon is mounted on is a Praga.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you say that it was 30 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was this type of weapon positioned around Sarajevo where you have indicated 30-millimetre anti-aircraft weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the Ilinjaca position, there's a sports airport position. At Klanac, and at position Y1, near the Slobodan Princip-Seljo barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. We note from the image that it appears to be a self-propelled vehicle. In other words, it has an engine and a driver. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In other words, it's a highly mobile weapon. It simply can be driven to the positions where it is required to fire from; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it it has four-wheel drive, or perhaps one might say six-wheel drive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please turn to the next photograph -- I withdraw that. Before we leave that photograph, how many of these units were in the SRK at, say, December 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 42, I think, in the entire Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, was this weapon able to operate in various modes? For instance, was it able to operate with the barrel kept pointing in the same direction, and was it also able to operate with the barrel moving as it fired successive shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barrel can rotate around its axis and it can be elevated. It can rotate by 360 degrees, regardless of the direction it rotates in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm asking you more particularly if it was able to rotate as it fired so as to project --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you mean by that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When firing, it moves to a minimal extent. As it opens fire, there is minimal movement. It depends how firmly the operator is holding onto the mechanism. But it doesn't move to a significant extent when it is being fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The primary purpose of a anti-aircraft weapon is to put up a wall of exploding rounds that an aircraft flies into; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To achieve that purpose, isn't every anti-aircraft gun capable of firing rounds in quick succession on a number of different -- slightly different trajectories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was this weapon capable of doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, what types of rounds was this weapon able to fire? You mentioned yesterday, for instance, that there were rounds fired by your weapons that would explode on impact. Is that a type of round that was fired from this weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main projectile was a momentary projectile. And out of 100 projectiles, only 10 per cent -- or rather, 8 per cent were not momentary ones, but they would explode only upon impact, or they would pierce armour that wasn't very thick, such as the armour on this weapon itself. I can point out that we used such armoured bullets in the course of combat action but not to a great extent, or rather, for most of the weapons we didn't even have such ammunition. We used so-called momentary projectiles, projectiles that would explode at the time of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As the transcript reads, you just said "we used so-called momentary projectiles, projectiles that would explode at the time of firing." Do you mean the time of firing or some other time that they would explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When they would hit the target or, rather, the obstacle. As I said yesterday, if it hit a curtain, it would explode because these were very -- this was a very sensitive type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And were they initially intended to explode on impact with an aircraft?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, what about the other 90 per cent of the shells? I take it they were not designed to explode on impact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 90 but up to 10 per cent of the armoured bullets, they wouldn't explode. They would only pierce armour that wasn't very thick. And they didn't explode upon impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I misunderstood your figures. Are you saying that 90 per cent were exploding projectiles? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And the remaining 10 per cent would not explode on impact; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Tell us about the remaining 10 per cent. What would they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as a rifle bullet, it's an ordinary bullet. It resembles a rifle bullet. When it hits an obstacle, if its force is sufficient, it will penetrate the obstacle. If the armour is thick or if there is a thick obstacle, a thick wall, then it couldn't do this. It could only inflict superficial damage on the obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you also have available to you incendiary rounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These so-called momentary projectiles are incendiary ones. They are at the same time incendiary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the ingredient is in the rounds that makes them incendiary? Is it a phosphorous?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a Trotil.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So if the round explodes on impact, then it also generates a lot of heat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heat is not -- it's not so hot, so it can't melt a metal obstacle. For example, if it hit a wall or stone or a brick, it wouldn't cause any damage apart from the damage resulting from the impact and the explosion. So the damage done to a wall is about this size, and it's about 2 or 3 centimetres deep. It doesn't destroy brick. It doesn't break through brick. It can only break through brick if there are successive shots at the same target. In theory this is possible, but in practice it's very difficult to inflict such damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the round would only cause a fire if it hit something that was inflammable? Not brick, but perhaps wood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you also have available to you for these weapons tracer rounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did -- I think the answer was no. Did you have available to you for any of the anti-aircraft weapons tracer rounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For 20-millimetre guns, yes. For the other smaller calibre that we will talk about later, it had tracer rounds, and you can see its trace which marks its trajectory when a series of bullets is fired, because it had an incendiary tracer at the rear end of the projectile. But the 30-millimetre projectiles, their traces can only be seen at night and not very well. They aren't visible during the day. You can only see the point that the projectile hits during the day, but you can't see its trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, was there another type of round that could be fired by that weapon, a round that was designed to explode in mid-flight even though it did not make contact with an object?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, all bullets can explode -- all projectiles can explode during the trajectory after they've covered part of its trajectory, the peak of its trajectory. And when the speed of the bullet starts diminishing, then the so-called self-liquidator is activated and the interior ignition is released to activate the projectile and to make it explode so that it's prevented from falling as armour-piercing [Realtime transcript read in error "armour pierces"] rounds on the ground. If you're firing above over your units, this is when one is applying a system to protect [Realtime transcript read in error "project"] one's own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did that apply to all of the ammunition that your anti-aircraft weapons fired; that is, all of the what you call momentary weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'm not quite sure, but I have to say it. I think we have to be very careful in terms of interpretation. And the answer as it was given by the witness in interpretation, on page 11, line 11, doesn't seem to be full. And I think tonight we have to look at it particularly carefully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately my laptop computer started a bit later, so I have to find the spot, page 11, 9/10. I have on page 11, lines 9 to 10 a question, rather than an answer. Line 11. Yes. Mr. DP35, I'll read to you a previous answer. And if it's not complete, would you please then complete. The answer you gave on a question whether there was a type of round that could be fired, a type of round that was designed to explode in mid-flight even though it did not make contact with an object, your answer was, "No. In fact, all bullets can explode -- all projectiles can explode during the trajectory after they've covered part of its trajectory, the peak of its trajectory. And when the speed of the bullet starts diminishing, then the so-called self --" I -- that's -- self-liquid, I think the translation was, "is activated and the interior ignition is released to activate the projectile and to make it explode so that its --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will. "So that it is prevented from falling as an armour pierces rounds on the ground if you're firing above your units. This is when one is applying a system to project one's own units." Does what I just read to you reflect the whole of your answer, or is there any part missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is fine, what you have read. Just what you can take out, the "no" at the beginning. Because what I understood the question to be was that -- the question was referring to the answer whether we were able to create a fire wall that we were talking about, the kind of barrage fire, with that self-liquidation, and we cannot do that. That's impossible. So there's no point to include "no" in the answer, because the self-liquidation is not happening at the same time because the barrage fire would be further away and further in depth. So I think the whole answer is fine except for the word "no." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So if I understand your evidence correctly, this characteristic applied to the rounds that were fired by your weapons that exploded on impact. In other words, if they didn't hit something and kept on travelling, then after the apex of their trajectory, they would explode in the air; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In air. So it doesn't fall to the ground. The bullets cannot reach the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you say that 90 per cent of the ammunition fired was of this type, was there a mixture of these sorts of rounds and non-exploding rounds in a burst of fire, or would the weapons fire a burst of the exploding rounds and later a burst of the non-exploding rounds? Were they mixed up or separate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear. It is not allowed to mix the ammunition. Precisely because of their different characteristics of the different rounds doing different trajectories in the air. So it is possible to have a magazine in some weapons with separate charges only in the case if there was a direct attack on the firing position with armoured weapons. That is why there were so few of that kind of ammunition. So, for instance, if I am being approached by armoured weapons directly to the firing position, then you take off the magazine with a momentary ammunition, and then you put on the armour-piecing ammunition in the magazine in order to repel the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And the armour-piercing ammunition is the -- was the non-exploding ammunition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you now move to the second photograph. Was this weapon --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- That was used by the SRK in September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a cannon 32/2 millimetres. We didn't have those kind of field guns, not in the JNA, not in the Republika Srpska army. That was probably used in some other countries. I, in fact, have never seen them in real life. I've only seen them like this, on a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Please move to the next photograph. So to save time during my questioning of you, I will refer -- you'll hear me refer to the relevant period. By that I mean the period between September 1992 and August 1994. Was this weapon ever in the SRK in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't exist before or after. This 40-millimetre or 70-millimetre weapon was only as part of the weapons of the airport. We didn't have that either in Butmir or in the area of Butmir airport such weapons. The closest such weapon could have been in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So the weapon did exist in the VRS but not in the SRK; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, please go to the next photograph. Was this weapon in the SRK in the relevant period for the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm referring --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please wait. For the transcript, I'm referring to the photograph which has in the top left-hand corner "20-3mm M55 AA gun." What type of weapon was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an anti-aircraft weapon. Our sign wasn't "AA gun." It's A4. We can see that it has magazines. This is where rounds are, twice 60 -- three magazines, 60 rounds each. It's got a calculation target device. It's more efficient to target targets in the air space. But when it is targeting targets on the ground, which it can be used for, then you do not use this calculating target device but you use a kind of binoculars or a telescope, an optical device which is used for also older kinds of weapons. It has a very high velocity of firing. It's a kind of weapon that we banned from using with all the three barrels that it had. But it was only used -- only the middle barrel was used in short bursts of fire in order to save ammunition. And its reach, successful, was up to 1500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the image we see some wheels and an axle in the background. Was it a gun that could be easily towed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the axle, which is the -- with the bottom half of the axle. This is the combat position, but when it is a marching position, it will be towed by a PAM 110, and then it would be towed in such a way it would move position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long would it take to transfer the weapon from its combat position to a mobile position ready to be towed away by --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I have to say it now. But I think that there was a problem in the French booth. Something didn't appear. So that's what we should pay attention to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if the French and the English compared while working on the transcript, proper attention will be paid to it. Is the English transcript complete in this respect, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? I didn't follow the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the English transcript seems complete, but what was said afterwards by the witness regarding the towing by PAM 110, that word that was said by the witness did not appear in the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it has been clarified now at least. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidentally, you told me earlier that in December 1993 there were approximately 42 of the 30-millimetre weapon, which is in the first image. Did that number remain constant between September 1992 and August 1994, or were there some changes? That's for the 30-millimetre, the Praga.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number didn't change significantly during this period except that during combat two weapons, I believe, during this period were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about the 20-millimetre that we see on the screen at the moment? How many of those did you have in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-four.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, is that just in the regiment, that is, the corps weaponry, or does that number include the weapons in the brigades as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the regiment, there were 16 of these weapons, and 8 of them were in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So throughout the entire SRK, there were a total of -- there were a total of 24 of these weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did this weapon have the same range of rounds as the 30-millimetre that you told us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this weapon was successful within the range of 1500 metres, and the other weapon, Praga, its successful range was up to 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But it could fire the explosive rounds, the non-explosive rounds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These weapons you would fire ammunition of three kinds: First the armour-piercing rounds. They were in a magazine of 12. Then there were the momentary rounds, so they would be 7 out of 12. And then 4 of 12, that is, one-third, would be the momentary incendiary tracer rounds. The armour-piercing, just like in Praga, were used only for immediate defensive tasks, and we had fewer than this amount, while these mixed rounds were such so that every fifth round was incendiary tracer momentary. The others were only incendiary. And the rest would depend on the circumstances. Sometimes these proportions would change, depending on the conditions, on the situation with the ammunition, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, these tracer rounds, could they be seen in daylight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we had at our disposal those incendiary momentary tracer ammunition, normally every battery should have that, depending on the levels of ammunition, but it would depend whether we had it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please turn now to the last photograph, that is, the next one. For the transcript, in the bottom left-hand corner, we see "40mm L60 AA gun."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it the top corner, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the SRK at any level possess this weapon in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This weapon is the same type as L70, which belonged only to the airport units, except that that was the new modification, and that's why it had "L70," and this has the code of L60.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So in this bundle of photographs, you have identified a 30-millimetre weapon and a 20-millimetre weapon as being in the SRK. You've told us also about a 40-millimetre weapon. I appreciate it is not the weapon in the photograph. Did it -- was it able to fire the same range of shells as the 30-millimetre weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't even possible for this ammunition L60/L70 to be fired. The weapon that we had, the 40-millimetre M1 weapon that we had, which is the production type and model M40, that is the model from 1940. It's an old type of ammunition with an optical sight and a specific -- its own specific type of ammunition. But as it happened, it happened to be there and it was there and it was one of the weapons that we had and we used, but we never used to fire the targets in the air but only exclusively targets on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did it have -- I'll withdraw that. Did it fire what you have called momentary rounds, that is, explosive rounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that weapon, M1, 40 millimetres, you did fire explosive rounds, momentary rounds. The magazine had eight rounds. That's how the field gun was loaded. And it normally had a lower velocity of firing compared to the other types of weapons that only used single firing, single mode, while the others only used bursts, burst mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the M40 was sometimes referred to as a Bofors gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's called Bofors because the producer is Bofors, and that's how the name stayed on both officially and popularly called Bofors. This weapon that we can see and the previous one is also made by Bofors, but this one was called Bofi as a more modern type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "this one," do you mean the one which appears on your screen at the moment or do you mean the M40 that you had in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The other one we called Bofors, the M1. While this one, L60, and what you also showed, the armoured vehicle -- the armoured weapon, L70, that's the Bofi, which has some modern modifications, particularly on the targeting device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, do you know of weapons -- sorry. I apologise. I have the flu. Do you know of weapons referred to as PAMs, P-A-M?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned it yesterday. PAM machine-gun, Browning type. I mentioned that Mojmilo had these weapons. As part of my units, we did not have a PAM because that is an infantry weapon which is used by the units of infantry for direct defence from air attacks. It is used and it can be used for firing targets on the ground, which I mentioned for the case of Mojmilo. But as I said, we didn't have it as part of our unit's weapons because it doesn't belong to the anti-air force weapons because it's a 12.7-millimetre calibre, while the anti-air force weapons should have a calibre of 20 millimetres upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, do you understand that some military people do regard 12.7-calibre machine-guns, in particular the PAM, as being anti-aircraft machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft machine-guns, yes. I always corrected my colleagues, saying that this was not an anti-aircraft weapon from the anti-air force defence but that it was an infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, coming back to the 40-millimetre weapon that you possessed. When that was firing repeatedly, can you give us some idea of the sound that it would produce. Could you describe that sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On what basis, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness should take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't know whether he understands any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then he can put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be appropriate in my respectful submission for the witness to leave the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the -- may I ask you, Mr. DP35, do you understand any English and/or French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would be sufficient if the witness takes off his earphones. And if you'd -- let me just confer for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the monitor of the witness be put on video rather than on the transcript. [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Gladly, Mr. President. Now, the testimony of the witness was regarding the 40-millimetre field guns, saying that they could not be firing in bursts of fire. That was in the transcript on the previous page, line 19. And now the question being asked is in contradiction of the testimony by the witness. I'm just looking for the page. But considering that we don't have the same pagination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what he said, yes. The witness was speaking of single shots, not of bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in my opinion the question was not regarding the bursts of fire but only about the noise that could be heard when this weapon was used. Perhaps this is a question of interpretation. But can you look at the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will just have a look at the screen. I was listening to the other channel. And perhaps I wasn't particularly careful regarding the transcript. What is the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see it. Thank you. It seems to me, as usual, Mr. President, that you are right. In this case, I withdraw the objection, Mr. President. No, no, no, Mr. President. What's being said -- I don't know whether the question as it was put was the firing repeatedly, whether it's to do with the bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen to the answer. [In English] Yes. Could, please, the headphones -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The 40-millimetre anti-aircraft gun that was in the SRK when fired repeatedly made what type of sound? Could you describe the sound that it made.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to describe sound. I can distinguish between different types of sounds when I hear them. A 20-millimetre gun when it is firing repeatedly has somewhat smaller sound, if we're talking about the nature of the sound. A 30-millimetre Praga fires in such a way that you hear the fire being opened and you hear a series of two projectiles being fired, and this isn't the case for a 20-millimetre gun. As far as a 40-millimetre gun is concerned, you can hear the fire being shot, like this, tup, tup, tup. Eight times in succession, if it fires all eight projectiles. It's louder than the noise made by the other guns and the sound is characteristic. I can recognise the guns when I hear these sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, apart from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, Mr. Ierace, and I'm also addressing the Defence, the tup, tup, tup sounds seem to me in a frequency of a little bit over one tup a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I agree with that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, apart from the three weapons that you've told us were in the SRK, that is, anti-aircraft weapons, were there any others? For example, you have identified the 30-millimetre anti-aircraft gun that appears on the first image in the bundle. Were there any other 30-millimetre anti-aircraft guns in the SRK in the relevant period apart from that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30-millimetre gun was only of this kind. There weren't any others. The 40-millimetre gun, there was only one type of this gun, of such a gun, and I've mentioned it. It's the M1. There were several types of 20-millimetre guns, in addition to the 20 through 3 millimetre guns, the A4s that we were able to see on the second photograph - not on this one - we had the 20 through 3 millimetre version in A3. It didn't have a targeting device, a calculating device, but it had an optical targeting device. And they belonged to the class of 20 through 3 weapons. In addition to those weapons, there were 20-millimetre M38 guns, one-barreled guns, two-barreled guns, and four-barreled guns. These were guns which were produced in Germany and remained on from the Second World War as trophies. They were popularly called Flak, F-L-A-K. The velocity of fire was not that high, and these are some of the weapons that remained in certain batteries. There were some 37-millimetre guns which resembled the M41 guns, and they belonged to the various batteries that were present there, and they were used to defend the positions of infantry units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The 37-millimetre guns, did you regard them as anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were categorised in that way, and the ammunition, if we had any ammunition, if we found any ammunition - but we couldn't gain supplies - I took control of 37-millimetre guns and Flaks and weapons that we took over from JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, I take it from your earlier answer that you did find some ammunition for the 37-millimetre guns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And you say that they were used -- I'm sorry, you say that they belonged to the various batteries and were used to defend the positions of infantry units. Do I take it that you had 37-millimetre guns at each of the positions that you marked on the map yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a total of 16 such guns in the entire corps. In the north-western part, in the brigade -- in the four brigades, it was possible to find three or four such weapons in one brigade. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "the north-western part," did you mark that position on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the part of the Igman Brigade and the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. I didn't mention the Ilijas Brigade, because it was further to the north on that map. So the part that I -- where I marked the positions with the letter "Y", the three or four or five positions that I marked, I think that you could find ten such weapons, ten such 37-millimetre guns at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier I asked you how many 20-millimetre guns of the type that appeared on the screen were in the SRK, and you said "24." How many 20-millimetre guns of whatever type --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Were in the SRK? Not just the A4s, but the various others you mentioned. How many in total 20-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were 24 A4 ones, 30 A3 guns, and I can't be precise but I think there were 15 or 16 20-millimetre guns of other types, one-barreled guns, two-barreled guns, and four-barreled guns, the so-called trophy guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, incidentally, did the SRK have machine-guns - I'm not talking about anti-aircraft machine-guns - with optical sights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about machine-guns with optical sights. I never saw such machine-guns. I only saw machine-guns with ordinary targeting devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do I take your answer to be that you don't know? You never saw any, but you don't know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you were asked whether there was a sniper unit within the SRK army corps, and you replied "no. Such unit did not exist, as far as I know." So were there any sniper units at any part of the structure of the SRK? I'm not asking just about the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. First of all, the Prosecution should seek to establish what the foundation of any knowledge that the witness might have is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The knowledge of the witness has been shown sufficiently. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, or do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the question. Yesterday I said that I wasn't familiar with this and that I never saw any sniper units. And similarly, I have now said that I never saw any machine-guns with optical sights. And I can state this because in the establishment of any of the units in the corps, within the corps brigades, there were no sniper units which existed. There were special units; that's the first thing I'd like to say. And secondly, when visiting the units and teams, I had the opportunity of seeing other units apart from the anti-aircraft defence equipment that they had. And in those units, too, I didn't see any weapons with optical sights and I didn't see any special units there either. And secondly, not at a single meeting when action was being prepared or not in a single report which I saw, I never found out that some sort of sniper unit was being used or that ammunition had been requested in order to arm such a unit. I know that as part of the establishment of sniping detachments there is one targetman who can be a sniper, but usually he wasn't a sniper if he didn't have a weapon with an optical device. It was usually the best marksman, and it was his duty to pay attention to some of the critical points because he was a better shot than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So are you telling us that you were aware that within the SRK --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness did not say a sniper detachment. It was a firing detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So are you telling us that as far as you are aware, there was no unit of snipers anywhere within the structure of the SRK in the relevant period? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suppose given your responsibilities, your daily tasks, occasionally fulfilling the role of operational duty officer, your high-level meetings with the corps commander over an extended period, if there had been such a unit, you would certainly know about it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So do you confidently tell us that there was no such unit in the SRK in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do make such a claim under oath and even if I'm not under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So you say that there may have been individuals, not snipers but the best marksmen in other units but not snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you say -- do you tell us that you never saw what might be called a sniper's rifle in the relevant period in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to object to this question before the witness answered it. It has to do with the fact that the Prosecution itself often states as its position that it's not necessary to talk about sniper weapons, in particular in order to talk about the issue of snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has become irrelevant because of the answer of the witness, I would say. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember saying a few moments ago, in relation to your visits to units and teams, "and in those units, too, I didn't see any weapons with optical sights and I didn't see any special units there either"? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see in the relevant period in the SRK what you understood to be an SRK specialist sniper weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw a captured one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday you said also that General Galic spent as much time in the operational headquarters as he did outside the operational headquarters. Firstly, were the operational headquarters at the Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you said that he spent time also at the forward command positions. Where were the forward command positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on need, in Butile, Nisici, in the surroundings of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could stop you there for a moment. Were the headquarters of each brigade effectively a forward command position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the brigades also had their permanent command positions and forward command positions. It depended on the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A forward command position has a temporary nature. It's a temporary position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, temporary in terms of the command position for the corps commander, but it may fulfil some other purpose in his absence from that position; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the focus of combat action is in the direction of Nisici, then it would be normal to expect there to be a forward command post there where part of the command or the staff would be located. Whether General Galic would be there or his deputy, that depended on the commander's decision. So the forward command post did not exist throughout the period. On the Nisici plateau, the forward command post was established in 1993, not before, and it was there until 1994, until General Galic -- sometime after General Galic left his duties. So it wasn't a matter of a tactical direction for the corps for the use of the units of the corps. That command post didn't even exist up until that day, up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That particular forward command post on the Nisici plateau, how far approximately, and in which position --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- From Lukavica was that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to the north of Lukavica, north of Vogosca. And the map that was here -- it's the northern part of the Sarajevo corps zone. In the map that we had a look at yesterday, it's up there, but it's difficult to explain now because we went in a round-about way. The route we took resembled the shape of an S to get there. Through Pale --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Approximately how far north of Vogosca was this particular forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20-odd kilometres to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Were there any forward command posts in the immediate vicinity of any part of the confrontation line around Sarajevo, apart from Lukavica itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Butile, which is near Rajlovac. They were there as command posts because -- they could be there before forward command posts in Nisici to control the activities and the combat of units such as the Ilijas or the 3rd Sarajevsko or the Igman Brigade, because it was cut off from Lukavica, or rather, Lukavica was cut off from that part of the battlefield, that zone. That was the closest location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you were required to do so by Mr. President, during the break could you mark on the map that you marked yesterday the forward command positions which were on territory included in that map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers the question, may I ask him to slow down a bit, because when answering the questions, you're speaking too quickly for the transcribers to catch all your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, again in relation to these daily meetings that took place at Lukavica that you attended, at which either General Galic himself led the meetings or a person, as I understand it, appointed by the chief of staff, did you ever see General Mladic present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those meetings of ours, which took place on a daily basis, no, General Mladic did not appear. But I did see General Mladic at meetings when there were reports from all commanders of the brigades and regiments. General Mladic would come to some of those meetings or some of the officers from the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where were those meetings held in the relevant period? Pale, at Lukavica, at different places? Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Lukavica, one was held. On Jahorina, at that time we didn't have such meetings in Pale. Mainly in Lukavica, the majority of meetings took place in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At those meetings, would General Mladic be briefed directly by the brigade commanders and relevant regiment commanders on the current situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The brigade commanders would report to General Galic, but General Mladic would follow the reporting at those meetings, and if necessary, if he so decided, he would ask a question if it seemed relevant to discuss this on the spot. So this would be in the course of a report or at the end he would assess the meeting and he would assign certain tasks to General Galic and to subordinated officers from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many such meetings were there in the relevant period that you attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure about one meeting, in September 1992, which was attended by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long after General Galic was appointed as corps commander was that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when General Galic was assuming the position as corps commander. I think it was the 6th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it more --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it more or less an introductory meeting? Did General Mladic introduce General Galic to the corps staff and the brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting at which he did introduce General Galic to us, those who were part of the corps. Politicians also participated in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was President Karadzic present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now. I know someone called Djeric was there from the government, a government representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A prime minister called Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't see the relevance of this matter, and this is why I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- it's a quarter to 4.00. Could I please ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom so that we could further hear the argument of the parties on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this is done, with your permission, the witness is going to be asked to mark positions on the map. What we want to suggest is that the witness traces the routes that were necessary in order to accede to these places from Lukavica base, so that we can see what difficulties their encountered and so that the witness can trace this on the map. If there are no objections, of course, on the part of the Prosecution and if this is something that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would expect usually to have asked this in redirect. But perhaps, Mr. Ierace, it would be -- since the witness mentioned it in cross-examination, would it be any objection if the witness would mark that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. DP35, we'll first grant you a short break because yesterday I think we put you to work on the break without even giving you an opportunity to go to the bathroom. So I'll first give you a short break. And would you then please mark during the rest of the time available, to mark the forward command positions on the map. And that should be done with a blue marker and then with a black marker to mark the routes to get to these forward command positions from Lukavica on that map. But I'll first give you an opportunity -- if at least the public gallery is empty, and may I instruct the technical booth not to put the witness on the video when he's leaving the courtroom. Madam Usher, may I ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please express the position of the Defence in relation to the relevance of the last objection about the presence of Mr. Karadzic during such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am under the impression that we are not adhering to the military framework. If we are asking questions about General Mladic, who was his superior in the military structure, we can understand that. But when we ask questions about other parties who weren't part of the military structure as such, so questions asked about civilians and about their role, this seems to be a different matter to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly is a different matter. But, Mr. Ierace, could you explain what the relevance of this question would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution case has always been that in carrying out the campaign against the civilians of Sarajevo, the accused was acting on orders from his immediate superiors, principally General Mladic. President Karadzic is part of that chain of command. You may also recall that we have heard evidence that the chief of staff of the VRS made a threat to a senior UN military official to attack civilian targets, namely trams, to shoot them. Given his position in relation to General Mladic and ultimately President Karadzic, it's certainly appropriate, in my respectful submission, to ask this witness whether those individuals were present at this key meeting where the accused is introduced for the first time to the senior -- his soon to be senior subordinates in the SRK and what was said. Mr. President, might I add to that, of course, the pre-existing nature of the campaign, which is alleged by the Prosecution, also makes it relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. It cannot be said that the question is without relevance for the Prosecution's case. Then we'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00. Could you indicate, Mr. Ierace, how much time you would still need for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have some difficulty in doing that. Excuse me. I imagine it would be at least another hour. If -- if you, Mr. President, and Your Honours are troubled by cross-examination going much longer than that, in view of the decision of the Defence to truncate its witness list, I'd seek some latitude with this witness, given his position in the corps; in other words, given the absence now of other senior subordinates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give it consideration. We'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that Mr. DP35 has marked the map during the break. Is that correct, Mr. DP35?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also was informed that not during the whole period of the marking both parties have been present. But I take it that there's no objection from any of the parties to accept that the markings are made by the witness. Then, Mr. Ierace, another issue about the time. You know that the Chamber has always refused to accept the banking system as such, but we'll apply some flexibility under the circumstances mentioned. And I'm just receiving now the -- you said you would need approximately one more hour. That would --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be an hour and a half. I find it difficult to answer these questions with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's the most helpful observation I can make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn for a small moment in order to give a decision, but we'll first give an opportunity to both parties to further discuss the time they would think proper to grant to the Prosecution -- the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could that be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It could be done in the absence of the witness. And I have -- I did not follow the Rules, Rules that are issued not by the Chamber. But the protection of witnesses is under the supervision of the Registry, and I am aware that the way I dealt with this as a Presiding Judge might cause some problems for those who have to follow these orders. So therefore, I would like to have the curtains be put down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before anything whatsoever, General Galic has asked me to request if it was possible for him to have a look at the marked map because he's the only who has not seen it, and I believe that that's an omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's not the only one. The Chamber has not seen it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, he is the only one on this side who has not seen the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can do that, and the time could be used for that. Mr. DP35, may I ask you to leave the courtroom for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Defence would have any contribution to the matter of how much time would be granted for cross-examination to the Prosecution, please address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Certainly. If I can just do it now in a few words. The first thing is that we can see that -- this year what the Defence allows itself to state. As far as we were concerned, there were fewer technical observations from the side of the Defence, and I hope that we are trying to be more selective and briefer in external manifestation of the objections that we have. That's the first thing. So today there was no time whatsoever that was lost. The second thing, the Prosecution took a lot of time to find out if the noise of the field gun did tup tup tup or put put put, et cetera, et cetera. But if it's this kind of questions, Mr. President, it seems to us that it doesn't have any kind of relevance on the question that we're interested in, which is the possible responsibility of General Galic. We have to -- here the questions are whether weapons were from the time of the Third Reich. That's the questions we were asked about. And these kinds of questions seem to be going too far. And if the Prosecution wishes to waste time in this way, they can do it, but they shouldn't ask any more time to have, because then we can just ask for another witness to come and testify. And if there is more of a delay, then we will have more problems with the witnesses. And the Defence would like to avoid that if possible. If additional time needs to be given, that is fine, but the Prosecution should be brief. This time should be used properly and concisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence takes the view that the level of relevance of the questions put to the witness until now do not justify additional time to be spent by the Prosecution on cross-examining the witness. That is a summary in three lines. Mr. Ierace, any ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, might I respond in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants one hour and 15 minutes for the Prosecution. We'll keep a close look on the clock for that. Madam Usher, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom and then the curtains be lifted again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst that's being done, in order to save time, might the map be placed on the ELMO, that is, the map marked by the witness. In particular, the area of Dobrinja on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could we perhaps first have a look at it and that solves the problem that the usher is not there to put the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, during the break you marked some of the forward positions, that is, forward command posts. On the map on the screen at the moment we see one of those being a triangle with the initials "KM," to the south-west of Dobrinja. Would you please point to it on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the command post. So that's without the "I" for the forward post.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please wait for the question. If you can concentrate on answering just the question, I'd be very grateful. What was that command post in? Was it a building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What type of building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A building in the barracks, in the building of the barracks. Before the war, that was the command, but not the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever go to that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. I object. That is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Just testified that this was not a forward command post but a command post. It's -- the witness said, "That's the command post. So that's without the 'I' for the forward post."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever go to that command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out my duty there, my basic task was there. That's where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was that throughout the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many storeys did the building have? Ground plus how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had another floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From that building, did you have a view of Dobrinja or any part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Dobrinja, what could be seen -- as you can see here, you can see Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And from that building, could you see the Dobrinja River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could the map be moved further to the right so that we can see more of the airport, please -- other direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. And slightly up, if the map could be moved -- other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday you marked two positions for anti-aircraft weaponry on a secondary runway which now appears on the map, is that correct, being X4 and X5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday also you gave us some evidence about an order that required SRK forces to open fire in certain circumstances at persons attempting to cross the airport in daytime or night-time. You told us that you never fired, that is -- Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17589 to 17592

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I'd just ask Mr. Ierace to be more precise as to where and when the witness said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Ierace is referring to an order which was shown to the witness. So the witness didn't say this, but the witness has answered questions in respect of such an order. Unfortunately, I haven't got the transcript of yesterday with me, but that's my clear recollection. It's one of the documents shown to him. So whether questions were put to him in that respect is a different matter, but a order was shown to him in which appears what Mr. Ierace just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Exhibit 14 - as far as I can read - 91. It's number 3 on this one-page document. But perhaps you could confront the witness with that part which has not been part of the testimony of the witness, although the witness has testified, I think, that he was aware of this order. But I don't think that specific part has been the subject of questioning, Mr. Ierace. Therefore, perhaps you could assist the witness in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the question I asked the witness was: Yesterday also you gave us some evidence about an order, and then went on to describe that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the time on my transcript, it's around 11.54.12 seconds. Mr. Piletta-Zanin showed him the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's no discussion as to whether it was shown to him, but sometimes orders are rather lengthy and not all aspects of an order -- at least it's not my recollection that this specific part of the order and the way you described that order was part of the questioning, of the examination of the witness. It was, rather, the other parts of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As I am not certain that the transcript reflects exactly the range of the order and item 3, I think it will be prudent, in fact even necessary, that Mr. Ierace read that or puts it on the ELMO so that we can all see what this is about. I do not think that there is a perfect reflection of what Mr. Ierace said, what's in the transcript, and the order as it was submitted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could the -- if you'd need to go into the content of that order, could perhaps the order be shown to the witness and that you put questions in respect of that order, unless you'd prefer not to do so for whatever reason, but -- it's not my recollection that the way you described the order was the subject of questioning and the testimony of the witness, so it might cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown D1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 1491. Thank you. That should be the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that yesterday the Defence counsel through the court orderly gave you this document and asked you to read it. He said to you, "Witness, would you please be so kind to read this document." Do you remember you were asked that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please look at paragraph 3. In particular --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In particular, the last sentence. Did the order require SRK forces in certain circumstances to open fire on persons crossing or attempting to cross the airport in the daytime or the night-time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it, and I don't interpret it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please read the last sentence slowly, on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We are trying to find --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "After discovering the same, as well as the citizens, individuals, motor vehicles and similar, who are intending to cross over the area of airport, especially if they are opening fire toward our positions, send immediately oral protest to the UNPROFOR and command of the UN forces at the airport, with the request to prevent it. In this case, open fire and decisively prevent such actions."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What do you disagree about what I suggested to you that order said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with what you said, that we are supposed to open fire on anyone who's going across the airport. Here it says that we are supposed to open fire but that the first thing we have to do is to address a protest to UNPROFOR before we do anything, and if we can't cross the airport, then obviously the Muslims shouldn't cross the airport either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I said to you that the order --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering the text that we have now and considering the fact that the Prosecution did not clearly indicate that this order was about responding to fire, I believe that the way that the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the question to the witness was whether this order contains an instruction to open fire under certain circumstances. The witness ignored that part of the question in his answer. And I think it's not proper to enter into a debate between the parties as to the content of this document at this moment, and the Prosecution should be allowed to put questions to the witness in that respect. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, the order sets out the circumstances in which fire is to be opened, those circumstances being where the SRK receives fire from those crossing the runway; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday did you also tell us that anti-aircraft weapons were never used on persons crossing the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you partake in the drafting of this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who it was, but the order was submitted and Dragan Marcetic signed it, who was at the time the deputy of the commander, that is, the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is it possible that Colonel Marcetic assisted you with the drafting of the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. He submitted it to me, he showed it to me -- I can't quite remember now. But it's almost ten years that have passed. I can't remember the details. It is possible that I -- that was written on the basis of the orders that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, was he the chief of staff of the SRK until the 20th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time he was. Whether he was chief of staff until June, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And as chief of staff, was he also the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, when you drafted this order, with whoever, which weapons did you contemplate would open fire on persons crossing the airport? If not anti-aircraft weapons, then which weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire can be opened on the airport runway only from the weapons that can have visibility towards the airport runway. The positions that I have marked, they do not have the conditions to open fire towards the airport runway across which the civilians were passing, were going across.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could the map please be placed back on the ELMO so that we can see the airport runway and its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take a pen - I think it's a blue pen - and mark the positions held by the SRK from which you expected fire could be directed onto the runway, in particular at persons crossing it in certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that I have marked on the sports airport, they were not in a position to do this, because they couldn't see the runway because --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I understand that, and you've told us that, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, I believe that there is a rule that when the witness is explaining something specific, he should not be interrupted. And if he is trying to tell us about the line of fire, then he should finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: If he's trying to tell us about the impossibility of the existence of the line of fire, then he should finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But Mr. President, may I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have given you an opportunity to respond to that, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you read my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin has misunderstood it. I have asked the witness to indicate the positions of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
